sections.h: 2 Maccabees 10: eight days "as one keeps the Feast of Booths"
sections.b: 2 Maccabees tells the cleansing of the Temple on 25 Kislev, the anniversary of its profaning, and the eight days of joy that followed (2 Maccabees 10:1–8). It explains the eight days by the Feast of Booths, which the fighters had missed while hiding in the mountains, and has them carry wands, branches and palms. The altar fire is struck from heated stones (2 Maccabees 10:3). A decree makes the days a yearly feast for the whole nation (2 Maccabees 10:8), and the letters at the front of the book urge the Jews of Egypt to keep it (2 Maccabees 1:9, 18). The oil that burned eight days appears only later, in the Talmud (Shabbat 21b).

sections.h: 2 Maccabees 10: Booths kept again in Kislev
sections.b: 2 Maccabees links the new feast of the Temple's cleansing with the Feast of Booths. The people kept eight days "as one keeps the Feast of Booths", because at the last Booths they had been living like wild animals in the mountains and caves, and they carried leafy wands, branches and palm fronds (2 Maccabees 10:6–7; Leviticus 23:40). Some historians think Hanukkah began as a delayed Booths; others point to Solomon's dedication at Booths (1 Kings 8:65–66).

2 Maccabees tells of heavenly horsemen who fight for Israel. Five splendid riders with golden bridles shield Judas and blind the enemy (2 Maccabees 10:29–30), and a rider in white with golden armor leads the army to Beth-zur after the people pray for "a good angel" (2 Maccabees 11:6–8). The book calls such events "appearances from heaven" (2 Maccabees 2:21; compare 3:25–26; 5:2–4). The 66 books know a heavenly army (2 Kings 6:17; Joshua 5:14), but only Revelation shows it riding to battle (Revelation 19:11–14).

Struck with an incurable disease, Antiochus IV confesses that a mortal must submit to God and vows to free Jerusalem, restore the Temple and even become a Jew (2 Maccabees 9:11–17). The writer says the Lord "was no longer going to have mercy on him" (2 Maccabees 9:13), and the king's letter that follows asks only for loyalty to his son. Christians have used the scene to ask whether sorrow from fear of punishment can be true repentance; the card on 2 Maccabees 9 gives Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and Reformed answers.

sections.h: 2 Maccabees 8: a pursuit broken off for the Sabbath
sections.b: After beating Nicanor, Judas's army stops chasing the enemy because the Sabbath is near, spends the day in praise, and shares out the spoils only when it is over (2 Maccabees 8:25–28). 1 Maccabees tells the same battle without the Sabbath (1 Maccabees 4:1–25), though it records the decision to fight back if attacked on that day (1 Maccabees 2:39–41). 2 Maccabees returns to the Sabbath after later battles (12:38) and when Nicanor plans to attack on it (15:1–5).

sections.h: 2 Maccabees 8–9: punishment that fits the crime
sections.b: 2 Maccabees likes punishments that mirror the crime. Callisthenes, who burned the Temple gates, is burned (2 Maccabees 8:33); Nicanor, who came to sell Jews as slaves, flees like a runaway slave (8:35); Antiochus, who tortured others' bowels, is struck in his own and eaten by worms (9:5–9). The writer says so: "It was perfectly just" (9:6). The pattern echoes the death of Jehoram (2 Chronicles 21:18–19).

sections.h: 2 Maccabees 8–11: the same war, in another order
sections.b: 2 Maccabees 8–11 covers the years told in 1 Maccabees 3–6, but in its own order. Judas beats Nicanor and Gorgias (2 Maccabees 8), Antiochus IV dies before the Temple is cleansed (9–10:9), and Lysias's defeat at Beth-zur comes after the cleansing, under the boy king (11:1–15), where 1 Maccabees puts it before (1 Maccabees 4:26–35). Four letters close the section (11:16–38); their dates suggest that the writer gathered the documents of the peace in one place.

sections.h: 2 Maccabees 9–11: from Antiochus IV to Eupator
sections.b: 2 Maccabees tells the end of Antiochus IV in the east (2 Maccabees 9), with a letter naming his son Antiochus V Eupator king (9:19–27). Lysias rules for the boy (10:11; 11:1), Ptolemy Macron is driven to suicide at court (10:12–13), and Philip flees to Egypt (9:29). The young king's letter to Lysias ends his father's policy of forcing Greek ways on the Jews (11:22–26).
